narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. We start with thousands of target stars, extract their brightness measurements over time, and search for the characteristic dips that occur when one star passes in front of another. Our pipeline applies statistical tests to distinguish likely eclipsing binaries from noise and instrumental artifacts, then cross-checks against six major variable-star catalogs to avoid re-listing already-known objects. Candidates that survive these checks go through an automated pixel-level image analysis - checking where in the TESS image the signal actually originates - to rule out a nearby star as the real source. We also score each candidate with a machine learning model, trained on the pipeline's own vetting history, as a second opinion alongside the rule-based checks; it does not currently decide which candidates get checked, and a high score is not a guarantee. So far we have identified 59 candidate eclipsing binaries this way, from a systematic search of the TESS target list. Some of these still have open caveats noted on their individual pages - this pipeline flags doubts rather than hiding them.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a system of two stars orbiting each other in such a way that, from Earth's perspective, one periodically passes in front of the other. When this happens, the total brightness of the system drops noticeably. By measuring these brightness dips we can infer properties like the orbital period and the relative sizes of the two stars. Measuring their masses precisely would require additional data, such as radial-velocity spectroscopy, which this pipeline does not collect.

faqs.question: What does 'candidate' mean here, versus 'confirmed'?
faqs.answer: A 'candidate' is a star whose light curve shows a statistical signature consistent with an eclipsing binary and passes our automated checks. A 'confirmed' candidate is one that has also passed an automated pixel-level image check, which rules out false signals caused by a nearby star or an instrumental artifact. Confirmed does not mean verified beyond this pipeline - some confirmed candidates still carry open caveats, which are listed on their individual pages.

faqs.question: What is the ML screening score, and what does it tell me?
faqs.answer: Our machine learning model, trained on the pipeline's own history of vetted candidates, estimates how likely a new candidate is to pass the same automated checks that earlier candidates passed or failed. A higher score means the model sees it as more similar to candidates that held up under vetting. This is a second opinion, not a gate - nothing in this pipeline currently uses the ML score to decide which candidates get checked, and the score is not a claim about whether a candidate is astrophysically real.

faqs.question: What is the 'pixel-level check,' and why do you do it?
faqs.answer: TESS observes many stars in a single image. Sometimes the brightness dip we measure actually comes from a nearby star, not our target. In the pixel-level check, the pipeline automatically examines where in the image the signal originates, to confirm it lines up with the intended target star rather than a neighbor. This step catches contaminants that the statistical tests alone might miss.

faqs.question: What if the signal looks like it could be an alias--a false period caused by the observation schedule?
faqs.answer: Period aliases are a real risk in any transit survey: the observation schedule can make eclipses look like they repeat at the wrong interval. We check for this with an odd/even test - comparing the depth of eclipses at alternating epochs. If the odd-numbered and even-numbered eclipses have significantly different depths, that is a signature of an alias, and we flag the candidate rather than silently correcting the period.

faqs.question: Can I verify one of these candidates myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each candidate on our site links to the underlying TESS light curve data and our analysis results, including which caveats, if any, are still open. You can download the data and examine it yourself using standard astronomy tools, and you can check our cross-match results against the public catalogs we use.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after you list it on this site?
faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter is the end of what this pipeline does - it does not mean a candidate has been published in the scientific literature or added to any official catalog. This is an automated result from TESS photometry and pixel-level image analysis only; no professional follow-up is built into this pipeline. A researcher could use a candidate here as a starting point for their own follow-up work, such as spectroscopy to measure masses, but that has not happened for any candidate listed here.
